explanation: Each face is one outcome and there are six faces, so the answer is 6. Twelve and thirty-six belong to two dice rather than one.

prompt: A bag holds one red, one blue and one green ball, and a single ball is taken out. What could the result be?
optionA: Red, blue or green
optionB: Red or blue only
optionC: Red, blue, green, or no ball at all
optionD: The number of balls left in the bag
correctAnswerText: Red, blue or green
explanation: Three balls give three possible results, one for each colour. Drawing nothing is not among them, because a ball is taken.

prompt: What does a sample space set out?
optionA: Only the outcomes that are reasonably likely
optionB: Only the outcomes somebody is interested in
optionC: Every outcome that could occur, each appearing once
optionD: The probability attached to each outcome
correctAnswerText: Every outcome that could occur, each appearing once
explanation: Completeness is the point: leaving out an unlikely outcome makes every probability computed from the list wrong. The probabilities themselves are a separate matter.

prompt: Two coins are tossed. A student says there are three possible results: two heads, two tails, and one of each. What has been missed?
optionA: Nothing; there really are three possible results
optionB: One of each can happen in two distinct ways, so there are four results rather than three
optionC: The result where neither coin lands at all
optionD: Nothing, since the order of the two coins does not matter
correctAnswerText: One of each can happen in two distinct ways, so there are four results rather than three
explanation: Head-then-tail and tail-then-head are different results even when nobody cares which coin did which. Collapsing them makes one of each look as likely as two heads, and it is twice as likely.

prompt: An ordinary die is rolled. Which results make up the event described as an even number?
optionA: 1, 3 and 5
optionB: 2 and 4
optionC: Every result from 1 to 6
optionD: 2, 4 and 6
correctAnswerText: 2, 4 and 6
explanation: Three of the six faces are even, so the event covers 2, 4 and 6. An event may hold several results at once, and this one holds three.

prompt: A card is taken from a pack holding only the numbers 1 to 10. The event of interest is described as more than 7. Which numbers does it cover?
optionC: 9 and 10
optionD: 1 to 7
explanation: More than 7 leaves 7 itself out and takes everything above it, giving 8, 9 and 10. The boundary value is where this kind of description is most often misread.

prompt: How many results can a single event cover?
optionA: Exactly one
optionB: At least two
optionC: Any number, from none of them up to all of them
optionD: At most half of what could happen
correctAnswerText: Any number, from none of them up to all of them
explanation: An event is simply a group of results, and a group may be empty, may hold one, or may hold everything. Nothing restricts its size.

prompt: A die is rolled and the event is described as at least 3. A student lists 4, 5 and 6. What is wrong?
optionA: Nothing; at least 3 does mean above 3
optionB: At least 3 takes in 3 itself, so the event is 3, 4, 5 and 6
optionC: The event should have been listed as 1, 2 and 3
optionD: At least 3 means exactly 3 and nothing else
correctAnswerText: At least 3 takes in 3 itself, so the event is 3, 4, 5 and 6
explanation: At least includes the value named, and more than excludes it. One face is the whole of the difference, and it changes the probability from a half to two thirds.

prompt: Which of these could not be a probability?
explanation: Nothing can be more certain than certain, and 1 is certainty, so 1.4 is impossible. Zero and one are both perfectly ordinary probabilities.

prompt: The probabilities of all the possible results of a trial are added up. What must the total come to?
optionD: The number of possible results
explanation: Something must happen, and the results cover everything that could, so the total is 1. A percentage is the same figure differently written.

prompt: A trial has three possible results, with probabilities given as 0.5, 0.3 and 0.1. Can that be right?
optionA: Yes, because each one lies between 0 and 1
optionB: Yes, because there are three results and three figures
optionC: No, because they total 0.9 rather than 1
optionD: No, because three results cannot have three different probabilities
correctAnswerText: No, because they total 0.9 rather than 1
explanation: Every figure is individually plausible and together they leave a tenth unaccounted for. Checking each value in isolation is exactly what lets this through.

prompt: A student defends a probability of 120 percent, saying percentages are allowed to exceed 100. What is wrong?
optionA: Nothing; percentages above 100 are perfectly normal
optionB: A probability can never pass the certainty of 1, however it happens to be written
optionC: It should have been written as a fraction instead
optionD: Percentages may not be used for probabilities at all
correctAnswerText: A probability can never pass the certainty of 1, however it happens to be written
explanation: Percentages above 100 are fine for growth and for comparisons, and a probability is neither. The limit belongs to the quantity, not to the notation.

prompt: An ordinary die is rolled once. What is the probability of an even number?
explanation: Three of the six faces are even, and 3 out of 6 is 1/2. Dividing the three favourable faces by the three unfavourable ones would give odds rather than a probability.

prompt: A bag holds 3 red and 5 blue balls, each equally likely to be picked. What is the probability of picking a red one?
explanation: There are eight balls altogether and three of them are red, giving 3/8. Dividing the reds by the blues gives 3/5, which counts against the wrong total.

prompt: The probability that a train is late is 0.2. What is the probability that it is not late?
explanation: The two possibilities together must come to 1, so the other is 0.8. Subtracting from 1 is the whole of the rule.

prompt: Two dice are rolled. Counting the ways of getting at least one six is awkward, but the probability of getting no six at all is known to be 25/36. What is the probability of at least one six?
explanation: At least one six is everything that is not no six, so it is 1 less 25/36, which is 11/36. The rule earns its keep exactly where the direct count is the harder one.

prompt: Five values are recorded: 4, 8, 6, 2 and 10. What is their mean?
explanation: The five total 30, and 30 shared among five is 6. Dividing by four instead would give 7.5.

prompt: Six values add up to 48 in total. What is their mean?
explanation: Sharing 48 among six gives 8. The individual values are not needed, because the mean depends on the total and the count and on nothing else about them.

prompt: A set of five values has a mean of 10. One of the values is increased by 20 and nothing else changes. The total rises by 20 and is still shared among the same five values, so the mean rises by 20 divided by 5. What is the new mean?
explanation: The mean climbs by four, from 10 to 14. Adding the whole 20 to the mean would be treating the change as though it happened to every value rather than to one.

prompt: The values 7, 2, 9, 4 and 5 are recorded in that order. What is their median?
explanation: Sorted they run 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, and the middle one is 5. Taking the middle of the list as written would have given 9, which is the largest value of the five.

prompt: Four readings are taken, in this order: 6, 1, 8 and 3. What is the median?
explanation: Sorted they run 1, 3, 6, 8, and with an even count the median is halfway between the two middle values, giving 4.5. Picking either middle value on its own is the usual shortcut.

prompt: The values 5, 2, 9, 2 and 7 are recorded in that order, and a student reports the median as 9 by taking the middle of the list as it stands. The median is the middle value once the list has been sorted, and this list is not in order. What is the median?
explanation: Sorted the values run 2, 2, 5, 7, 9, so the middle one is 5. The figure 4.6 is the mean, which answers a different question about the same values.

prompt: Two groups of five values have the same mean. The first is 9, 10, 10, 10, 11 and the second is 2, 6, 10, 14, 18. Which is more spread out?
optionA: The first
optionB: Neither; an equal mean means an equal spread
optionC: The second
optionD: It cannot be told from what is given
correctAnswerText: The second
explanation: Both average 10, and the second reaches from 2 to 18 where the first barely leaves 10. The shared mean is precisely what makes the difference here visible as spread.

prompt: Two groups each have a mean of 20. One runs from 19 to 21 and the other from 5 to 35. What does the mean on its own tell you about how varied they are?
optionA: That the two are equally varied
optionB: Nothing; the mean is identical while the variation is entirely different
optionC: That the first is the more varied of the two
optionD: That the second contains more values than the first
correctAnswerText: Nothing; the mean is identical while the variation is entirely different
explanation: A centre says where values sit and says nothing about how far they scatter around it. Any question about variation needs a figure that measures variation.

prompt: Two delivery teams report the same mean time of 30 minutes. One delivers between 28 and 32 minutes and the other between 5 and 55. A customer wants to know whether a delivery might take an hour, and the mean is identical for the two teams while their longest times are not. Which figure answers the customer?
optionA: The mean, since it summarises both teams in one number
optionB: The number of deliveries each team has made
optionC: Neither; the question cannot be answered from figures like these
optionD: A figure describing the spread, since the means cannot tell the two teams apart
correctAnswerText: A figure describing the spread, since the means cannot tell the two teams apart
explanation: The customer is asking about the far end of the range, and the two teams differ entirely there while agreeing exactly at the centre. Reporting only the mean would answer a question nobody asked.

prompt: A die is rolled. The probability of a 1 is 1/6 and of a 2 is 1/6, and the two cannot both happen on one roll. What is the probability of a 1 or a 2?
explanation: Results that cannot both occur simply add, giving 2/6, which is 1/3. Multiplying them would answer a question about two rolls rather than one.

prompt: In a group, the probability that someone plays cricket is 0.6 and that they play football is 0.5. A student adds the two and reports 1.1. What is wrong?
optionA: Nothing; 1.1 is a perfectly valid probability
optionB: The two figures should have been multiplied rather than added
optionC: The two can both be true of one person, so adding counts those who play both twice
optionD: The two figures given must themselves be wrong
correctAnswerText: The two can both be true of one person, so adding counts those who play both twice
explanation: A total above 1 is the visible symptom, and the cause is that adding assumes the two cannot happen together. Here they plainly can.

prompt: The probability that a customer buys tea is 0.4, that they buy coffee is 0.3, and that they buy both is 0.1. Adding 0.4 and 0.3 counts the 0.1 who buy both once in each figure, so one copy of them has to come off. What is the probability that a customer buys at least one of the two?
explanation: Seven tenths less one tenth leaves 0.6. Multiplying the two figures would give 0.12 and answers a question about independence, which nothing here has claimed.

prompt: A coin is tossed twice, and neither toss affects the other. What is the probability of two heads?
explanation: Two independent halves multiply, giving 1/4. Adding the two instead would make two heads certain, which no pair of coin tosses is.

prompt: A bag holds 4 red and 6 blue balls. One ball is drawn and put back, and then a second is drawn. Are the two draws independent of each other?
optionA: Yes, because replacing the ball restores the bag to how it started
optionB: No, because the same bag is used on both occasions
optionC: No, because the first draw changes what is left
optionD: Only when the two balls drawn are the same colour
correctAnswerText: Yes, because replacing the ball restores the bag to how it started
explanation: Replacement is what makes the second draw face exactly the situation the first did. Without it the counts would have changed and the draws would not be independent.

prompt: A bag holds 3 red and 7 blue balls, and two are drawn without replacement. A student computes the probability of two reds as 3/10 times 3/10. The first ball is not put back, so by the second draw the bag holds 9 balls of which at most 2 are red. What is the correct probability?
explanation: The second draw faces 2 reds among 9, so the answer is 3/10 times 2/9, which is 1/15. Multiplying is right and the second figure is not.

prompt: Nine people earn 20,000 each and one earns 500,000. Which summary better describes what a typical person earns?
optionA: The mean, because it takes every earner into account
optionB: The median, because one enormous value drags the mean away from everybody
optionC: Neither; the two give the same answer here
optionD: The largest value, since it is the most striking figure
correctAnswerText: The median, because one enormous value drags the mean away from everybody
explanation: The mean comes out near 68,000, which nobody earns. The median stays at 20,000, which nine of the ten actually earn.

prompt: A set of values has a mean of 12 and a median of 11. One further value of 300 is added to it. A single value far above the rest moves the mean substantially and shifts the median by at most one position. What happens to the two summaries?
optionA: Both of them rise sharply
optionB: The median rises sharply and the mean barely moves
optionC: Neither changes, since one extra value cannot matter
optionD: The mean rises sharply and the median barely moves
correctAnswerText: The mean rises sharply and the median barely moves
explanation: The mean absorbs the whole of the 300 and shares it out; the median only steps along the sorted list by one place. That difference is what makes the median the safer summary for skewed data.

prompt: A fair coin has landed heads six times running. A gambler says tails is now due. Is that right?
optionA: No; the coin has no memory and the next toss is still an even chance
optionB: Yes, because results have to balance out in the end
optionC: Yes, because a run of six is very unlikely to continue
optionD: It depends on how carefully the coin is being tossed
correctAnswerText: No; the coin has no memory and the next toss is still an even chance
explanation: Six heads in a row is unlikely in advance and has already happened, which changes nothing about the seventh toss. The coin carries no record of what it did before.

prompt: Cards are dealt from a single pack without replacement, and all four aces have already appeared. A player says a further ace is now less likely. Because the cards are not put back, every ace dealt is one fewer ace remaining in the pack. Is the player right?
optionA: No; each deal is independent of the ones before it
optionB: No; the probability of an ace never changes
optionC: Yes; with no aces left the probability is now zero, because the deals are not independent
optionD: Yes, but only because the pack is reshuffled between deals
correctAnswerText: Yes; with no aces left the probability is now zero, because the deals are not independent
explanation: This is the case where the same-sounding claim is correct, and what makes it correct is that the cards are not replaced. A coin would have been a different matter entirely.

prompt: Two collections of values turn out to have the same mean. What follows about the individual values in them?
optionA: They must contain the same values as each other
optionB: Very little; the two may look entirely unlike each other
optionC: They must contain the same number of values
optionD: At least one value must appear in both
correctAnswerText: Very little; the two may look entirely unlike each other
explanation: A mean constrains the total and leaves everything else free. Two collections sharing one can differ in size, in spread and in every individual value.

prompt: A class has a mean mark of 50, and a student concludes that somebody must have scored close to 50. A mean of 50 can be produced by marks of 0 and 100 alone, with nobody anywhere near the middle. Is the conclusion sound?
optionA: Yes; the mean is always near at least one of the values
optionB: Yes, provided the class is reasonably large
optionC: No, but only when the class has an even number of students
optionD: No; the mean need not be close to any individual value
correctAnswerText: No; the mean need not be close to any individual value
explanation: The mean is where the values balance, not where any of them sits. A class split between two extremes has a mean nobody scored.

prompt: Two collections of five values share both a mean of 10 and a median of 10, and a team concludes that the two must be identical. Sharing a centre and a middle value still leaves the values on either side free to be anything at all. Is the conclusion right?
optionA: No; two very different collections can share both figures
optionB: Yes; a shared mean and median together fix the values
optionC: Yes, provided both collections hold five values
optionD: No, but only if the two collections are of different sizes
correctAnswerText: No; two very different collections can share both figures
explanation: The set 10, 10, 10, 10, 10 and the set 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 agree on both figures and agree on nothing else. Two summaries pin down two things, and five values need more than two.

prompt: A dashboard reports one average response time of 200 milliseconds, and users complain of long waits. The average covers every request, and a small fraction of very slow requests barely moves an average taken over a great many fast ones. What should be reported instead?
optionA: The same average, recomputed more frequently
optionB: The total number of requests handled
optionC: A figure describing the slow end, such as the worst few percent
optionD: The fastest response time on record
correctAnswerText: A figure describing the slow end, such as the worst few percent
explanation: The complaints are about the tail and the average is dominated by the body. Reporting the worst few percent measures the thing users are actually experiencing.

prompt: A report states that the mean number of children per family is 2.3, and a reader objects that no family has 2.3 children. A mean is a total shared out and need not be a value any individual could take. Is the objection sound?
optionA: Yes; the figure should have been rounded to 2
optionB: No; a mean need not be a value that any individual could have
optionC: Yes; a mean is not a valid summary for things that are counted
optionD: No, though the median would suffer from the same problem
correctAnswerText: No; a mean need not be a value that any individual could have
explanation: The figure describes the group rather than any family in it, and rounding it would lose real information about the group. The median here would be a whole number, which is exactly why it does not have this problem.

prompt: A town reports house prices. Most houses sell for between 20 and 40 lakh and three sell for over 500 lakh. Someone asks what a typical house costs, and the three very expensive sales pull the mean well above anything most buyers will see. Which summary should be reported?
optionA: The mean, because it takes every sale into account
optionB: The mode, because it names the price that came up most often
optionC: The highest price, since it shows how far the market reaches
optionD: The median, because it is not dragged upwards by the three extreme sales
correctAnswerText: The median, because it is not dragged upwards by the three extreme sales
explanation: Every option is correctly computed and only one answers the question asked. Typical is what the median is for, and skew is exactly when the two summaries part company.

prompt: A hospital must publish a summary of waiting times. The mean is easy to explain to the public; the worst few percent is what determines whether anyone waits dangerously long. Both figures are correct. Which should lead the report?
optionA: The worst few percent, because the decision the report informs is about dangerous waits
optionB: The mean, because the public will understand it more readily
optionC: The mean, because it takes every waiting time into account
optionD: Neither; the raw waiting times should be published without any summary
correctAnswerText: The worst few percent, because the decision the report informs is about dangerous waits
explanation: What the report is for decides which figure leads. Understandability matters and cannot outrank answering the question the report exists to answer.

prompt: A shop wants to know which shirt size to stock most heavily, and has the size of every sale. The question is about the single size that comes up most often rather than about a centre or a spread. Which summary answers it?
optionA: The mean
optionB: The median
optionC: The mode
optionD: The range
correctAnswerText: The mode
explanation: Stocking is decided by what sells most, which is what the mode reports. A mean of the sizes could easily name a size nobody buys.

prompt: A team reports the mode of a set of times, each measured to the nearest thousandth of a second. Almost no two of the values repeat, and the mode turns out to be a value that happened to occur twice. What is wrong with reporting it?
optionA: Nothing; the mode is always a valid thing to report
optionB: A mode means little where values hardly ever repeat, and this one is a coincidence
optionC: The values should have been rounded before the mode was taken
optionD: A mean should never be used for measurements of time
correctAnswerText: A mode means little where values hardly ever repeat, and this one is a coincidence
explanation: A mode is informative when repetition is meaningful, and at that precision it is not. Rounding first would produce a mode worth reporting and is a different decision that has to be made deliberately.

prompt: A monthly report can carry one summary figure or three. One fits the front page and hides how varied the month was; three fill a section that few readers will study. The report is read by managers who act on it the same day. What is the reasonable choice?
optionA: One figure, because managers have no time to study three
optionB: Three figures, because more information is always better
optionC: One figure, provided that the figure chosen is the mean
optionD: A centre and a spread together, since one figure alone would hide what the managers must act on
correctAnswerText: A centre and a spread together, since one figure alone would hide what the managers must act on
explanation: Two figures answer both where the month sat and how varied it was, which is what acting on it requires. More is not automatically better, and neither is less.

prompt: A survey of 12 students in one class finds that 75 percent prefer online classes, and the result is reported as the view of the university. All twelve come from a single class, and nothing about that class was chosen to resemble the university as a whole. Is the conclusion warranted?
optionA: No, because the students surveyed were not chosen to represent the university
optionB: Yes, because 75 percent is a clear majority
optionC: Yes, because the arithmetic behind the percentage is correct
optionD: No, purely because twelve students is too small a number
correctAnswerText: No, because the students surveyed were not chosen to represent the university
explanation: Selection is the fault here rather than size. Twelve students chosen at random from across the university would support a weak conclusion; twelve from one class support none.

prompt: A website invites visitors to rate it, and 90 percent of those who respond rate it highly. The team reports that 90 percent of visitors are satisfied. Only visitors who chose to respond are counted, and whether someone chooses to respond may itself depend on how satisfied they are. What is wrong?
optionA: Nothing; 90 percent of respondents is 90 percent of visitors
optionB: The number of respondents is too small to report
optionC: The respondents selected themselves, so they need not resemble visitors as a whole
optionD: The rating scale must have been designed badly
correctAnswerText: The respondents selected themselves, so they need not resemble visitors as a whole
explanation: The people who answer are a group shaped by the very thing being measured. The figure is a true statement about respondents and an unsupported one about visitors.

prompt: A trial of a new process runs on 2,000 randomly chosen orders and shows a small improvement. A reviewer rejects the finding on the grounds that all sampling is unreliable. The sample is large and was chosen at random, which is precisely the situation in which a sample does support a conclusion. Is the rejection reasonable?
optionA: Yes; no sample can support a conclusion about the whole
optionB: No; a large random sample is exactly what makes a conclusion supportable
optionC: Yes, unless every order was included in the trial
optionD: No, but only if the improvement had been larger
correctAnswerText: No; a large random sample is exactly what makes a conclusion supportable
explanation: Rejecting every sample is as unreasoning as accepting every one. This sample has both of the properties that make sampling work, and the reviewer has engaged with neither.

prompt: A team can survey 100 people chosen at random at real cost, or 10,000 volunteers reached through a link at almost none. The larger group is not chosen at random and the smaller one is, and the question is what the whole population thinks. Which is the better basis?
optionA: The 10,000, because a larger sample is always the more reliable
optionB: The 10,000, because the money saved can fund further surveys
optionC: Either, since both are samples drawn from the same population
optionD: The 100 chosen at random, because size cannot repair a group that was never chosen to represent
correctAnswerText: The 100 chosen at random, because size cannot repair a group that was never chosen to represent
explanation: A bigger unrepresentative sample measures its own bias more precisely and gets no closer to the population. Random selection is what buys the link to the whole, and nothing else substitutes for it.

prompt: Which of these is a statement that is either true or false?
optionA: Close the door
optionB: The number 7 is greater than 5
optionC: What time does the train leave?
optionD: Please try again later
correctAnswerText: The number 7 is greater than 5
explanation: Only the first makes a claim that could be checked and found right or wrong. A command and a question assert nothing, so there is nothing in them to be true.

prompt: Which of these carries no truth value at all?
optionA: The report was sent yesterday
optionB: The report has 12 pages
optionC: No report was sent
optionD: Please send the report
correctAnswerText: Please send the report
explanation: A request is not a claim about how things are, so it cannot be true or false. The other three all assert something that could turn out either way.

prompt: Is "It will rain in Chennai tomorrow" a statement that is either true or false?
optionA: Yes, though which of the two it is cannot yet be known
optionB: No, because nobody knows yet
optionC: No, because it is about the future rather than the present
optionD: Yes, and as things stand it is true
correctAnswerText: Yes, though which of the two it is cannot yet be known
explanation: The sentence makes a definite claim, and tomorrow will settle it one way or the other. Not knowing the answer is a fact about us, not about the sentence.

prompt: A sentence qualifies when it makes a claim that is either true or false. Which of the following qualifies?
optionA: Restart the server at midnight
optionB: Should the server restart at midnight?
optionC: The server restarted at midnight
optionD: Restarting servers at midnight is inconvenient
correctAnswerText: The server restarted at midnight
explanation: Only the first reports something that either happened or did not. The last is an expression of preference, which cannot be settled by checking anything.

prompt: A student says that "The millionth digit of pi is 7" does not count, because nobody in the room knows whether it is true. What is wrong with that?
optionA: Nothing; a sentence nobody can check does not count
optionB: Having a truth value is not the same as anyone knowing it; the sentence is one or the other regardless
optionC: It does not count, but for a different reason entirely
optionD: It counts only once somebody has actually computed the digit
correctAnswerText: Having a truth value is not the same as anyone knowing it; the sentence is one or the other regardless
explanation: The digit is whatever it is, and the sentence is true or false accordingly. Availability of the answer is a separate matter from the existence of one.

prompt: A rule applies when a customer is a member and also holds a voucher. Which connective does that use?
optionA: OR
optionB: NOT
optionC: It uses no connective at all
optionD: AND
correctAnswerText: AND
explanation: Both requirements have to hold of the same customer, which is what AND expresses. OR would admit members with no voucher.

prompt: A discount is offered to anyone who is a student or a pensioner. Someone is both. Does the discount apply to them?
optionA: Yes; OR in logic includes the case where both parts hold
optionB: No, because or means one or the other but not both
optionC: Only if the offer explicitly adds the words or both
optionD: It cannot be decided from the offer as written
correctAnswerText: Yes; OR in logic includes the case where both parts hold
explanation: The OR of logic asks for at least one, so satisfying two is more than enough. Everyday speech often means the exclusive version, which is the source of the confusion.

prompt: Which connective reverses the truth value of whatever it is applied to?
optionA: AND
optionB: OR
optionC: NOT
optionD: IF
correctAnswerText: NOT
explanation: NOT turns true into false and false into true, and is the only one of the four that acts on a single statement rather than joining two.

prompt: A sign reads: free entry for children or seniors. A child who is also a senior is turned away, on the grounds that the word or excludes anyone who is both. Is the refusal supported by logic?
optionA: Yes, because or always excludes the case where both hold
optionB: No; the OR of logic admits those who satisfy both conditions
optionC: Yes, because no person can genuinely be in both categories
optionD: It depends on which of the two categories the sign listed first
correctAnswerText: No; the OR of logic admits those who satisfy both conditions
explanation: Satisfying either condition is what the sign asks for, and this person satisfies two. The exclusive reading is a habit of speech rather than anything the wording requires.

prompt: A truth table is drawn up for a statement with 2 variables. How many rows does it have?
explanation: Each variable can be true or false independently, giving two times two, which is 4. The number of variables is not itself the number of rows.

prompt: How does the number of rows in a truth table change when one more variable is added?
optionA: It doubles
optionB: It increases by one
optionC: It increases by two
optionD: It stays the same
correctAnswerText: It doubles
explanation: Every existing combination appears twice over, once with the new variable true and once with it false, so the count doubles. That is why tables become unwieldy so quickly.

prompt: A truth table lists every combination of values its variables can take. What must be true of its rows?
optionA: Only the combinations making the statement true appear
optionB: The rows may be as many or as few as convenient
optionC: Every combination appears exactly once
optionD: The combination where every variable is false is left out
correctAnswerText: Every combination appears exactly once
explanation: Completeness is the point of the table: leaving a combination out is exactly how an expression gets mistaken for one it merely resembles.

prompt: A student draws a table for a statement with 3 variables and writes 6 rows. What has gone wrong?
optionA: Nothing; 6 rows is right for 3 variables
optionB: Each variable doubles the count, so 3 variables need 8 rows
optionC: The student should have written 9 rows
optionD: The student should have written 3 rows, one for each variable
correctAnswerText: Each variable doubles the count, so 3 variables need 8 rows
explanation: Multiplying the variable count by two gives 6 and squaring it gives 9; neither is how the combinations grow. Doubling three times from a single row is what gives 8.

prompt: A system keeps two flags for each order, shipped and invoiced. For one order the shipped flag holds and the invoiced flag does not. What does the combined requirement shipped and invoiced come to for that order?
optionA: True
optionB: It cannot be determined
optionC: Both outcomes at once
optionD: False
correctAnswerText: False
explanation: A requirement of both parts fails as soon as one fails, so the answer is False. Both flags have been given values, which leaves nothing undetermined.

prompt: Three flags describe a booking: paid holds, cancelled does not, and confirmed holds. What does the requirement paid, together with either cancelled or confirmed, come to?
optionA: True
optionB: False
optionC: It cannot be determined
optionD: It depends which of the two inner flags is checked first
correctAnswerText: True
explanation: Either of the inner flags is enough and confirmed holds, so the inner part succeeds; paid holds as well, so the whole comes to True. Checking order cannot change a result the grouping has already fixed.

prompt: Two sensors are wired so that an engineer can ask whether it is not the case that both report a fault. On this occasion both sensors do report a fault. What does that denial come to?
optionA: True
optionB: It cannot be determined
optionC: False
optionD: It depends which of the two sensors is considered
correctAnswerText: False
explanation: The statement being denied holds, so the denial of it is False. The denial covers the pair taken together rather than either sensor on its own.

prompt: A condition is written so that a negation covers only the first of two parts joined by AND. The first part is true and the second is false. What does the whole condition come to?
optionA: True
optionB: False
optionC: It cannot be determined without knowing the connective
optionD: It would be false only if the negation had covered both parts
correctAnswerText: False
explanation: Negating the true first part gives false, and false joined by AND to anything is False. Both halves fail here, which is why the answer is unaffected by the second part.

prompt: The statement is: if it is raining then the match is cancelled. It is not raining, and the match went ahead. Is the statement false?
optionA: Yes, because the match was not cancelled
optionB: Yes, because the two parts of the statement disagree
optionC: It cannot be decided from a single day
optionD: No; a statement of this form is not broken when its first part is false
correctAnswerText: No; a statement of this form is not broken when its first part is false
explanation: The statement promises something only about rainy days. A dry day on which the match is played is not a case it ever spoke about.

prompt: The statement is: if the light is red then the car stops. The light is green and the car stops anyway. Has the statement been broken?
optionA: No; the first part is false, so nothing was promised about this case
optionB: Yes, because the car stopped when the light was not red
optionC: Yes, because a green light should mean the car does not stop
optionD: It cannot be decided without watching more cars
correctAnswerText: No; the first part is false, so nothing was promised about this case
explanation: Only a red light followed by a car that fails to stop would break it. Stopping at green is unremarkable and outside what the statement covers.

prompt: A rule reads: if a form is late then a fee is charged. A form arrived on time and a fee was charged anyway. A statement of this form is false only when the first part is true and the second is false, and here the first part is false. Has the rule been broken?
optionA: Yes, because a fee was charged without any lateness
optionB: Yes, because the rule implies that punctual forms attract no fee
optionC: No, because the rule says nothing about forms that arrive on time
optionD: It cannot be decided from a single form
correctAnswerText: No, because the rule says nothing about forms that arrive on time
explanation: Reading the rule as forbidding a fee on punctual forms is reading its converse, which it does not assert. The fee may be unfair, and it is not a breach of this rule.

prompt: Take the four rows for P and Q in this order: both true; P true and Q false; P false and Q true; both false. What is the column for P OR Q?
optionA: True, False, False, False
optionB: True, True, True, False
optionC: False, True, True, True
optionD: True, True, False, False
correctAnswerText: True, True, True, False
explanation: OR is true wherever at least one part is true, which is the first three rows, and false only in the last: True, True, True, False.

prompt: Over the four rows taken in the order both true, P only, Q only, neither, one column reads True, False, False, False. Which expression produces it?
optionA: P OR Q
optionB: NOT (P AND Q)
optionC: P on its own
optionD: P AND Q
correctAnswerText: P AND Q
explanation: Being true in the single row where both hold is the signature of P AND Q. P on its own would also be true in the row where only P holds.

prompt: A column over the rows both true, P only, Q only, neither reads True, True, True, False. A colleague calls it the column for P AND Q. The column is true in three rows out of four, whereas an AND is true only in the row where both parts hold. Which expression is it?
optionA: P OR Q
optionB: P AND Q
optionC: NOT P
optionD: P AND NOT Q
correctAnswerText: P OR Q
explanation: Three true rows out of four is what OR gives, and one true row is what AND gives. Counting the true rows is enough to rule the claim out before checking any row individually.

prompt: Are P AND Q and Q AND P equivalent?
optionA: No, because the two parts are written in a different order
optionB: Only when P and Q happen to have the same value
optionC: Yes, they agree on every row
optionD: It cannot be decided without being given values
correctAnswerText: Yes, they agree on every row
explanation: Requiring both parts does not depend on which is named first, so the two columns match everywhere. Equivalence is settled by the table, not by appearance.

prompt: Are NOT (P AND Q) and NOT P AND NOT Q equivalent?
optionA: Yes, since a negation passes through an AND unchanged
optionB: No; they differ whenever exactly one of P and Q is true
optionC: Yes, they agree on all four rows
optionD: No; they differ only in the row where both are true
correctAnswerText: No; they differ whenever exactly one of P and Q is true
explanation: With P true and Q false the first comes to true and the second to false. In the row where both are true the two agree, which is why checking that row alone proves nothing.

prompt: A developer checks whether P OR (P AND Q) is equivalent to P by trying three cases: both true, P true with Q false, and both false. The three cases tried leave out the row where P is false and Q is true, which is the only row where the two could have come apart. What has the check established?
optionA: That the two are equivalent, since three rows out of four agreed
optionB: That the two are not equivalent
optionC: That the two are equivalent whenever P is true
optionD: Nothing conclusive, because the row the check needed is the one it omitted
correctAnswerText: Nothing conclusive, because the row the check needed is the one it omitted
explanation: The three rows tried were never in doubt. Whether the claim happens to be true is a separate question from whether this check settled it, and it did not.

prompt: The statement is: if a number is a multiple of 4 then it is even. What is its converse?
optionA: If a number is even then it is a multiple of 4
optionB: If a number is not a multiple of 4 then it is not even
optionC: If a number is not even then it is not a multiple of 4
optionD: A number is a multiple of 4 and is also even
correctAnswerText: If a number is even then it is a multiple of 4
explanation: The converse swaps the two parts and leaves them unnegated. It is a different claim, and here a false one, since 6 is even and is not a multiple of 4.

prompt: Which restatement of "if it is a dog then it is a mammal" says exactly the same thing?
optionA: If it is a mammal then it is a dog
optionB: If it is not a dog then it is not a mammal
optionC: If it is not a mammal then it is not a dog
optionD: It is a dog and it is a mammal
correctAnswerText: If it is not a mammal then it is not a dog
explanation: Swapping the parts and negating both leaves the meaning untouched. Doing only one of those two operations changes what is being claimed.

prompt: A policy says: if an account is dormant then it is archived. A team implements it by treating every archived account as dormant. Treating every archived account as dormant is the converse of the policy, which the policy does not assert. What has gone wrong?
optionA: The contrapositive has been implemented in place of the policy
optionB: The converse has been implemented as though it followed from the policy
optionC: Nothing; reversing a policy says the same thing
optionD: The policy as written is self-contradictory
correctAnswerText: The converse has been implemented as though it followed from the policy
explanation: Accounts may be archived for reasons other than dormancy, and the policy leaves room for that. The contrapositive, that anything not archived is not dormant, would have been sound.

prompt: A branch runs when a user is logged in and has confirmed their email address. A user is logged in but has not confirmed. Does the branch run?
optionA: Yes, because one of the two parts holds
optionB: Yes, because being logged in is the more important requirement
optionC: It cannot be decided from what is given
optionD: No, because both parts must hold
correctAnswerText: No, because both parts must hold
explanation: A requirement of both fails as soon as one part fails. Neither part outranks the other; they are simply both required.

prompt: A branch runs when an order is overdue or flagged. An order is neither overdue nor flagged, though it is unusually large. Does the branch run?
optionA: No, because neither of the two named parts holds
optionB: Yes, because the order is unusually large
optionC: Yes, because a requirement of either kind needs only one thing to be true
optionD: It cannot be decided without knowing the order value
correctAnswerText: No, because neither of the two named parts holds
explanation: Size is not one of the two conditions, so it cannot satisfy either. Needing only one part is true and useless when neither part is present.

prompt: A branch is meant to run for users who are either administrators or auditors, and it is running for every user in the system. Every user satisfies at least one of the two conditions as they are currently written, because the auditor condition was written so that it holds of everyone. Why does the branch always run?
optionA: Because AND was used where OR was intended
optionB: Because the administrator condition is true of every user
optionC: Because one of the two parts is true of every user, and only one is needed
optionD: Because any branch with two conditions runs for everyone
correctAnswerText: Because one of the two parts is true of every user, and only one is needed
explanation: An always-true part makes the whole always true, whatever the other part does. Using AND would have produced too few users rather than too many.

prompt: What is the value of P OR NOT P?
optionA: False, whatever P is
optionB: True, whatever P is
optionC: True only when P is true
optionD: It depends on the value of P
correctAnswerText: True, whatever P is
explanation: One of the two parts holds in each of the two possible cases, so the whole comes to True either way. There is no value of P that makes both parts fail.

prompt: An expression built from P and Q comes out true on three of its four rows and false on the fourth. A developer describes it as always true. Being false on one row is enough to make a claim of always true wrong, however many rows agree. Which description is correct?
optionA: It is always true
optionB: It is always false
optionC: It is true whenever P is true
optionD: It depends on the values of P and Q
correctAnswerText: It depends on the values of P and Q
explanation: Three rows out of four is not every row, and an expression that varies at all depends on its variables. Which row fails has not been stated, so nothing more specific can be said.

prompt: A filter should show orders that are urgent and unpaid. It is showing urgent orders, paid ones included. Which fault fits?
optionA: The unpaid part is not being applied
optionB: The urgent part is not being applied
optionC: A requirement of either was used where both were needed
optionD: Both parts have been negated
correctAnswerText: The unpaid part is not being applied
explanation: Everything shown is urgent, so that part is working. Paid orders getting through means the second requirement is having no effect at all.

prompt: A rule should grant access to staff who are full-time and have completed training. It is granting access to every full-time member of staff, including those who have not completed training, and to nobody else. Nobody outside the full-time group is being granted access, so that part is working. What is the fault?
optionA: The full-time requirement is not being applied
optionB: A requirement of either was used where both were needed
optionC: The training requirement is not being applied at all
optionD: Both parts of the condition have been negated
correctAnswerText: The training requirement is not being applied at all
explanation: Had either part been enough, trained part-time staff would have been let in too, and the stem says nobody outside the full-time group gets access. That rules the loosened requirement out and leaves the training check doing nothing.

prompt: A branch runs when a user is both verified and active. The opposite branch runs whenever that requirement fails. Which users take the opposite branch?
optionA: Only those who are both unverified and inactive
optionB: Those who are unverified, or inactive, or both
optionC: Only those who are unverified
optionD: Nobody, since the two branches cover the same users
correctAnswerText: Those who are unverified, or inactive, or both
explanation: A requirement of both fails as soon as either part fails, so failing one is enough. Requiring both failures would leave a verified but inactive user with no branch to take.

prompt: A requirement is that a file be both readable and recent. Its denial has been written as "not readable and not recent". A file that is readable but old fails the original requirement, and the denial as written does not admit it. What is wrong with the denial?
optionA: The denial should have kept the connective and negated neither part
optionB: The denial is correct exactly as written
optionC: The two parts of the denial should have been written in the other order
optionD: Denying a requirement of both gives not readable or not recent, with the connective changed
correctAnswerText: Denying a requirement of both gives not readable or not recent, with the connective changed
explanation: Negating the parts without changing the connective is the half-done rule, and it admits only files that fail on both counts. The readable-but-old file is precisely the case it loses.

prompt: A rule admits anyone who is either a member or a subscriber. Someone asks which people the denial of that rule admits. Satisfying even one part would have satisfied the original rule, so the denial can admit nobody who satisfies either. Who does the denial admit?
optionA: Only those who are neither a member nor a subscriber
optionB: Those who are not a member, or not a subscriber, or both
optionC: Those who are both a member and a subscriber
optionD: Nobody at all
correctAnswerText: Only those who are neither a member nor a subscriber
explanation: Denying a requirement of either gives a requirement of neither, which is much narrower than the original. The loose-sounding option would admit a member who is not a subscriber, and the original rule already admitted them.

prompt: An alert fires when a service is down and not under maintenance. A team wants the exact set of situations in which the alert does not fire. Not firing means the two-part requirement failed, and a two-part requirement fails as soon as either part does. Which situations are they?
optionA: The service being up and under maintenance at the same time
optionB: The service being up, and nothing else
optionC: The service being up, or the service being under maintenance, or both
optionD: The service being under maintenance, and nothing else
correctAnswerText: The service being up, or the service being under maintenance, or both
explanation: Either failure is enough, so the quiet cases are the union of the two rather than their overlap. Listing only one of them would leave the team blind to half of their silent periods.

prompt: A requirement is that a value be greater than 10 and less than 20. A developer denies it as at most 10 and at least 20. No value can be both at most 10 and at least 20, so the denial as written admits nothing whatever. What is wrong?
optionA: The comparisons should have excluded the boundary values
optionB: The connective should have become or, so that failing either comparison is enough
optionC: The denial is right and the original requirement was wrong
optionD: The two comparisons should have been written in the other order
correctAnswerText: The connective should have become or, so that failing either comparison is enough
explanation: A denial that can never hold is a reliable sign that the connective was left alone. Every value outside the range fails one comparison or the other, and none fails both.

prompt: A refund is allowed for orders that are unopened or faulty. An order that is both unopened and faulty must also qualify, and an order that is opened and not faulty must not. Which condition expresses the rule exactly?
optionA: Unopened and faulty
optionB: Unopened or faulty, but not both
optionC: Unopened, with faulty ignored
optionD: Unopened or faulty
correctAnswerText: Unopened or faulty
explanation: Either ground is sufficient, and having two grounds does not disqualify anyone. Excluding the both case would deny a refund to the customer with the strongest claim.

prompt: A prize goes to entrants who answered every question or finished within the time limit, but not to those who did both, since they go into a separate draw. Entrants who did both must be excluded even though each part on its own would admit them. Which condition is right?
optionA: Exactly one of the two, and not both
optionB: Either of the two, the both case included
optionC: Both of the two together
optionD: Neither of the two
correctAnswerText: Exactly one of the two, and not both
explanation: Neither part can be used unmodified, since each admits the very entrants who must be excluded. Only the exclusive form leaves them out while keeping everyone else.

prompt: A notification should reach users who have opted in and have a verified address. Users who opted in without verifying must not be contacted, and users who verified without opting in must not be contacted either. Which condition expresses that?
optionA: Opted in or verified
optionB: Opted in or verified, but not both
optionC: Opted in and verified
optionD: Verified, with opting in ignored
correctAnswerText: Opted in and verified
explanation: Each one-sided case is named in the requirement as excluded, so both parts are necessary. A requirement of either would contact exactly the two groups the rule rules out.

prompt: Access is granted to staff who are not on leave. One member of staff has no leave record at all. Having no record is a different thing from having a record that shows no leave, and the rule says nothing about which of the two an absent record represents. What should be done?
optionA: Treat the missing record as meaning the person is on leave
optionB: The rule must say how a missing record is to be read before the condition can be written
optionC: Treat the missing record as meaning the person is not on leave
optionD: Refuse access whenever a record is missing
correctAnswerText: The rule must say how a missing record is to be read before the condition can be written
explanation: Either reading is a decision with consequences, and picking one silently buries it in code. The gap is in the rule, and it is the rule that has to close it.

prompt: A condition can be written as the denial of a two-part requirement, or as two denials joined the other way. The two admit exactly the same cases. One form will be read by people thinking in terms of the original requirement, the other by people who will later extend it with a third part. What should decide between them?
optionA: The first, because fewer negations are always clearer
optionB: The second, because it is closer to the order a machine evaluates in
optionC: Neither; a condition of this shape should be split into two separate rules
optionD: Either is correct, so the choice turns on which form the people maintaining it will read more reliably
correctAnswerText: Either is correct, so the choice turns on which form the people maintaining it will read more reliably
explanation: Correctness cannot separate them, so nothing about the logic settles it. Claiming that one form is always clearer replaces a judgement about these readers with a rule that does not hold generally.

prompt: A building admits someone who holds a valid pass and appears on the visitor list for today. A contractor holds a valid pass and appears on yesterday list. Holding a valid pass satisfies only one of the two requirements, and both are required. Is the contractor admitted?
optionA: No, because only one of the two requirements is satisfied
optionB: Yes, because the valid pass is the substantive requirement
optionC: Yes, because appearing on a visitor list at all is enough
optionD: It cannot be decided from the rules as given
correctAnswerText: No, because only one of the two requirements is satisfied
explanation: Both requirements are stated, so satisfying one leaves the person outside. Yesterday list is not today list, however similar the two look.

prompt: A refund system applies three rules that must all hold: the item was bought within 30 days, it is unused, and a receipt exists. A customer has a receipt and bought the item 10 days ago, but has used it. All three rules must hold together, and one of them does not. What is the outcome?
optionA: A refund, since two of the three rules are satisfied
optionB: A partial refund in proportion to the rules satisfied
optionC: No refund, because a requirement that all three hold fails as soon as one does
optionD: It cannot be decided without knowing what the item cost
correctAnswerText: No refund, because a requirement that all three hold fails as soon as one does
explanation: Requirements joined this way are not scored; they are met or not met. Two out of three is a failure in exactly the same way that none out of three is.

prompt: A discount applies when a customer is not a first-time buyer. A new system holds no record of whether a given customer has bought before. The absence of a record is being read as proof that the customer has not bought before, which is a different claim from a record showing no previous purchase. What is the risk?
optionA: Every customer will end up receiving the discount
optionB: Returning customers whose history the system never received will be treated as first-time buyers
optionC: No customer will end up receiving the discount
optionD: The discount will be applied twice to some customers
correctAnswerText: Returning customers whose history the system never received will be treated as first-time buyers
explanation: Not knowing something is being treated as knowing it to be false, and the two differ exactly for customers whose history was never loaded. Those are the people the rule will get wrong.

prompt: An eligibility rule can be stated as one condition with four parts, or as four separate checks each with its own message. The single condition is quicker to evaluate and tells a rejected applicant nothing about which part they failed. Applicants must be told why they were rejected. Which form fits?
optionA: The single condition, because it is quicker to evaluate
optionB: The single condition, with one general message covering all four parts
optionC: Either, since the two reach the same decision
optionD: The four separate checks, because the requirement includes telling the applicant which part failed
correctAnswerText: The four separate checks, because the requirement includes telling the applicant which part failed
explanation: Both forms decide identically, so the decision is not what separates them. One of them can meet the stated obligation to explain and the other cannot.

prompt: Paris is the capital of France. If the first position holds the city and the second the country, which ordered pair records that?
optionA: (France, Paris)
optionB: (Paris, France)
optionC: {Paris, France}
optionD: (Paris, Paris)
correctAnswerText: (Paris, France)
explanation: The convention stated puts the city first, so (Paris, France) is the record. Swapping the two says that France is the capital of Paris, which is a different claim rather than the same one written differently.

prompt: A record is written as (7, 2), where the first position holds a student number and the second holds a mark. What does the 7 stand for?
optionA: The mark
optionB: Either one, since a pair carries no fixed order
optionC: The number of students recorded
optionD: The student number
correctAnswerText: The student number
explanation: The positions were assigned meanings before anything was written, so the first value is the student number. Without that convention the record would say nothing at all.

prompt: Does (3, 8) mean the same as (8, 3)?
optionA: No, because the two positions carry different meanings
optionB: Yes, because both contain 3 and 8
optionC: Yes, as long as the two values are of the same kind
optionD: Only when the pair is written between braces instead
correctAnswerText: No, because the two positions carry different meanings
explanation: Order is the entire content of an ordered pair beyond the values themselves. Two collections containing 3 and 8 would be the same; two ordered pairs are not.

prompt: A delivery log pairs a driver with the van they drove, driver first. Sunil drove van 12. Which pair records it?
optionA: (12, Sunil)
optionB: (Sunil, Sunil)
optionC: (Sunil, 12)
correctAnswerText: (Sunil, 12)
explanation: Driver first means (Sunil, 12). The reversed form would be read by anything using this log as a van having driven a person.

prompt: A system stores pairs of the form (manager, report), manager first. A record reads (Anya, Ben), and a colleague reads it as meaning that Ben manages Anya. What has gone wrong?
optionA: Nothing; a record of this kind may be read in either direction
optionB: The positions were read in the wrong order, so the record actually says Anya manages Ben
optionC: The record itself is wrong and should have been written as (Ben, Anya)
optionD: The record should have used braces rather than brackets
correctAnswerText: The positions were read in the wrong order, so the record actually says Anya manages Ben
explanation: The data is correct and the reading is not. A convention that is not carried to the reader turns every record into two contradictory claims.

prompt: A mapping is given by the pairs (1, 5), (2, 7) and (3, 5). What is its domain?
explanation: The domain holds the values that go in, which are 1, 2 and 3. The values 5 and 7 are what comes out, and belong to the range.

prompt: A machine turns 10 into a, 20 into b, and 30 into a. Which values come out of it?
optionA: {a, b}
optionC: {a, b, a}
correctAnswerText: {a, b}
explanation: Only a and b ever emerge, and a emerging twice does not make it two different outputs. The numbers going in are a separate collection entirely.

prompt: In a mapping, what is the domain?
optionA: The values that come out
optionB: The pairs themselves
optionC: The values that go in
optionD: The number of pairs
correctAnswerText: The values that go in
explanation: The domain is the collection of inputs. The outputs form the range, and confusing the two reverses every question asked about the mapping.

prompt: A mapping sends 1 to 4, 2 to 4 and 3 to 9. A student gives its range as {4, 4, 9}. What is wrong?
optionA: Nothing; the range really is {4, 4, 9}
optionB: The range is a collection of the values produced, so 4 is listed once, giving {4, 9}
optionC: The range should have been given as {1, 2, 3}
optionD: The range should have been given as {1, 2, 3, 4, 9}
correctAnswerText: The range is a collection of the values produced, so 4 is listed once, giving {4, 9}
explanation: Two inputs producing 4 does not put 4 into the range twice, because a collection of this kind records what belongs to it rather than how often.

prompt: A relation contains the pairs (1, 5), (2, 5) and (3, 8). Is it a function?
optionA: No, because 5 comes out of two different inputs
optionB: No, because there are three pairs but only two different outputs
optionC: It cannot be decided from the pairs alone
optionD: Yes; every input appears once, and two inputs sharing an output is allowed
correctAnswerText: Yes; every input appears once, and two inputs sharing an output is allowed
explanation: Each of 1, 2 and 3 has exactly one output, which is the whole requirement. That 1 and 2 both produce 5 breaks nothing.

prompt: Each student is recorded with a tutor. Riya appears twice, once with tutor Das and once with tutor Mehta. Does this record define a mapping from students to tutors?
optionA: No, because one student has been given two different tutors
optionB: Yes, because every student named has a tutor
optionC: No, because two students are not allowed to share a tutor
optionD: Yes, because the two entries for Riya can simply be merged
correctAnswerText: No, because one student has been given two different tutors
explanation: One input with two outputs is exactly what a mapping forbids. Merging the entries is not available, since Das and Mehta are different tutors and the record does not say which is right.

prompt: Which situation stops a mapping from being a function?
optionA: Two inputs having the same output
optionB: An output that is never produced
optionC: One input having two different outputs
optionD: Having more inputs than outputs
correctAnswerText: One input having two different outputs
explanation: The requirement is one output per input, so only a repeated input with disagreeing outputs breaks it. The other three are all perfectly ordinary.

prompt: A student rejects the pairs (1, 7), (2, 7) and (3, 9) as not being a function, because 7 appears twice. What is wrong with that reasoning?
optionA: Nothing; an output appearing twice does disqualify it
optionB: A shared output is allowed; only a repeated input with different outputs disqualifies a mapping
optionC: It fails for a different reason, namely that 9 appears only once
optionD: A collection of three pairs can never be a function
correctAnswerText: A shared output is allowed; only a repeated input with different outputs disqualifies a mapping
explanation: The student has applied the rule to the wrong side of the pair. Reading it correctly, no input repeats at all, so nothing here is in question.

prompt: A rule doubles its input and then adds 3. What comes out when 5 goes in?
explanation: Doubling 5 gives 10 and adding 3 gives 13. Adding first and then doubling gives 16, which is what happens when the two steps are taken in the other order.

prompt: A rule subtracts 2 from its input and then multiplies the result by 4. What comes out when 6 goes in?
explanation: Six less 2 is 4, and 4 multiplied by 4 is 16. Multiplying first and subtracting afterwards gives 22 instead.

prompt: A mapping is given as a table: 1 goes to red, 2 goes to blue, 3 goes to red. What does 3 go to?
optionA: blue
optionC: red
optionD: Both red and blue
correctAnswerText: red
explanation: The row for 3 gives red. That red also appears in the row for 1 changes nothing about what 3 produces.

prompt: A price table lists small at 40, medium at 60 and large at 90. A customer asks the price of an extra-large. What does the table give?
optionA: 90, since it is the largest size listed
optionB: Nothing, because extra-large is outside what the table covers
optionC: 130, by continuing the pattern of the sizes
optionD: 40, since the first row acts as a default
correctAnswerText: Nothing, because extra-large is outside what the table covers
explanation: A mapping says nothing about an input it does not contain. Extending the pattern or reaching for a default is a decision someone would have to make, not something the table already says.

prompt: A mapping sends 1 to a, 2 to b and 3 to c. Is it one-to-one?
optionA: No, because it contains three separate pairs
optionB: Yes, because every input has exactly one output
optionC: It cannot be decided without being told the range
optionD: Yes, because no two inputs share an output
correctAnswerText: Yes, because no two inputs share an output
explanation: Being one-to-one means no output is reached twice, and here a, b and c are all different. Every input having one output is true of every mapping and settles nothing.

prompt: A mapping sends 1 to 4, 2 to 9 and 3 to 4. Is it one-to-one, and what decides it?
optionA: No; 1 and 3 both produce 4
optionB: Yes; every input still has exactly one output
optionC: No; 2 produces 9 and nothing else produces 9
optionD: It cannot be decided from only three pairs
correctAnswerText: No; 1 and 3 both produce 4
explanation: Two different inputs arriving at 4 is precisely the failure. The pair that produces 9 uniquely is the part that works, not the part that breaks.

prompt: A membership scheme records each member against their home branch. No member is recorded against more than one branch, and two members who live near each other are both recorded against the same branch. A shared branch means two inputs producing the same output, which is not what disqualifies a function but is what disqualifies a one-to-one mapping. Which is true?
optionA: It is neither a function nor one-to-one
optionB: It is one-to-one but not a function
optionC: It is a function but not one-to-one
optionD: It is both a function and one-to-one
correctAnswerText: It is a function but not one-to-one
explanation: One output per member makes it a function; two members reaching one branch stops it being one-to-one. The two conditions are about opposite sides of the pair, which is why a mapping can satisfy one and fail the other.

prompt: A rule squares each value in the collection {-2, -1, 0, 1, 2}. Which values does it actually produce?
explanation: Squaring gives 4, 1, 0, 1 and 4, so the values produced are {0, 1, 4}. The inputs themselves are a different collection, and 2 never comes out at all.

prompt: A rule squares its input and is permitted to produce any whole number at all. Which of these can it never produce?
optionA: Zero
optionB: A very large number
optionC: An odd number
optionD: A negative number
correctAnswerText: A negative number
explanation: Squaring never yields a negative number, whatever the rule is permitted to produce. Being allowed to produce a value and actually producing it are different things, and this is the gap between them.

prompt: A grading rule is permitted to output any whole number from 0 to 100, and it works by multiplying a whole-number mark out of 20 by five. Because the input is a whole number out of 20, only multiples of five ever come out, though every value from 0 to 100 is permitted. Which values does the rule actually produce?
optionA: Only the multiples of five from 0 to 100
optionB: Every whole number from 0 to 100
optionC: Every whole number from 0 to 20
optionD: Only the even numbers from 0 to 100
correctAnswerText: Only the multiples of five from 0 to 100
explanation: Twenty-one inputs give twenty-one outputs, so most of the permitted values never appear. A report that quoted the permitted values as the possible results would be describing something the rule cannot do.

prompt: One machine adds 1 to whatever it is given, and a second machine doubles whatever it is given. The value 3 is fed to the first and its result to the second. What comes out?
explanation: Three becomes 4, and 4 doubled is 8. Feeding the machines in the other order gives 7, which is why the order has to be stated.

prompt: A checkout takes 10 rupees off a price and then a service charge doubles whatever remains. A price of 50 is processed. What is charged?
explanation: Fifty less 10 is 40, and doubling gives 80. Doubling before the deduction would give 90, so the customer pays 10 more for the same two operations.

prompt: A checkout should deduct 10 rupees and then double what remains. On a price of 50 the intended charge is 80, and the system reports 90. The two orders differ because the deduction is not being carried through the doubling. Which order is the system using?
optionA: Deducting first, then doubling
optionB: Both operations applied to the original price separately
optionC: Only the doubling, with the deduction never applied
optionD: Doubling first, then deducting
correctAnswerText: Doubling first, then deducting
explanation: Doubling 50 gives 100, and deducting 10 leaves the 90 that was reported. Applying only the doubling would have given 100, which rules that reading out.

prompt: A mapping sends 1 to a, 2 to b and 3 to c. Can it be reversed so that each output leads back to exactly one input?
optionA: Yes, because no output is shared
optionB: No, because a mapping can never be run backwards
optionC: No, because there are three inputs to account for
optionD: Only if the outputs happen to be numbers
correctAnswerText: Yes, because no output is shared
explanation: Each of a, b and c is reached by exactly one input, so each has somewhere unambiguous to return to. Reversal is possible precisely when that is true.

prompt: A reading scheme puts Asha on shelf x, Boro on shelf y and Chen on shelf x. Can the scheme be run backwards, so that naming a shelf identifies one reader?
optionA: Yes, by writing each assignment the other way round
optionB: Yes, so long as the readers are taken in alphabetical order
optionC: No, because shelf x would have to identify both Asha and Chen
optionD: No, because shelf y has been given to only one reader
correctAnswerText: No, because shelf x would have to identify both Asha and Chen
explanation: Writing the assignments backwards is easy; getting a single reader out of shelf x is not. That shelf y behaves perfectly does not rescue the scheme, since the property has to hold everywhere.

prompt: A system records each order against the month it was placed. Many orders share a month. Given only a month, no single order can be recovered, which is exactly the condition that stops a mapping being reversible in this sense. Can the mapping from orders to months be reversed so that a month leads back to one order?
optionA: Yes, by listing every order placed in that month
optionB: No, because a month cannot lead back to one order
optionC: Yes, because every order has exactly one month
optionD: No, because months are not numbers and cannot be reversed
correctAnswerText: No, because a month cannot lead back to one order
explanation: Listing every order for a month is a useful thing to do and is not a reversal, since it returns many answers where one was required. The forward direction being well defined is what makes the failure easy to miss.

prompt: A lookup structure stores one value against each key, and a key may appear only once. Read as a mapping, what plays the part of the inputs?
optionA: The values
optionB: Both the keys and the values together
optionC: The number of entries stored
optionD: The keys
correctAnswerText: The keys
explanation: A key is what is supplied and a value is what comes back, so the keys are the inputs. Reversing the two turns every question about the structure inside out.

prompt: A lookup stores the value 7 against key A and the same value 7 against key B. Read as a mapping, is it a function?
optionA: Yes, because each key still leads to exactly one value
optionB: No, because the value 7 is stored twice
optionC: No, because two keys are not permitted to share a value
optionD: Only once the two keys have been merged into one
correctAnswerText: Yes, because each key still leads to exactly one value
explanation: The requirement constrains keys, not values. Two keys arriving at the same value is the same situation as two inputs sharing an output, which has never been forbidden.

prompt: A store allows the same key to be written twice with different values, and a read returns whichever was written most recently. The same key can therefore produce two different values depending on when it is read, which is precisely what a mapping may not do. Read as a mapping, what is it?
optionA: A function, because a read always returns exactly one value
optionB: A function, because the most recent write settles the matter
optionC: Not a function, because one input can give different outputs
optionD: Not a function, because two keys are able to share a value
correctAnswerText: Not a function, because one input can give different outputs
explanation: A single read returning one value is not the same as the key having one value. Time is the second input here, and once it is admitted the structure stops being a mapping from keys alone.

prompt: A relation contains (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (2, 5) and (4, 3). Which pair stops it being a function?
optionA: (4, 3), because 3 appears as an output twice
optionB: (2, 5), because 2 already appears with 3
optionC: (3, 4), because it is the reverse of (4, 3)
optionD: (1, 2), because 2 appears as both an input and an output
correctAnswerText: (2, 5), because 2 already appears with 3
explanation: The input 2 leads to 3 in one pair and to 5 in another, which is the only conflict present. The other three pairs are unusual to look at and break nothing.

prompt: A register of 4,000 entries maps staff numbers to departments and turns out not to be a function. Exactly one staff number appears twice, once against Sales and once against Support; every other staff number appears once. One repeated input with two different departments is enough to disqualify the whole register however large it is. What needs fixing?
optionA: Every entry, since the register as a whole is now unreliable
optionB: The department names, which need to be made unique
optionC: Nothing; a register of this size is expected to contain repeats
optionD: The single staff number recorded against two departments
correctAnswerText: The single staff number recorded against two departments
explanation: Three thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine entries are correct. The property is all-or-nothing, which makes the register fail entirely and the repair very small.

prompt: Two steps should run in order: take away 5, then multiply by 3. For an input of 20 the expected result is 45, and the system reports 55. What explains it?
optionA: The two steps ran in the other order
optionB: The multiplication used 4 rather than 3
optionC: The input was 25 rather than 20
optionD: The subtraction was applied twice over
correctAnswerText: The two steps ran in the other order
explanation: Multiplying 20 by 3 gives 60, and taking away 5 leaves the 55 that was reported. No single wrong value produces that figure with the steps in the right order.

prompt: A pipeline should trim the spaces from a name and then take its first three characters. Given two spaces followed by Ravi, the expected result is Rav, but the system returns three characters beginning with two spaces. A result beginning with spaces shows the trimming had not happened when the characters were taken. What is wrong?
optionA: The trimming step is removing the wrong characters
optionB: The system is taking four characters rather than three
optionC: The two steps are running in the wrong order
optionD: The input contains characters other than the ones described
correctAnswerText: The two steps are running in the wrong order
explanation: Taking the first three characters first yields two spaces and an R, which is exactly what was observed. Trimming afterwards cannot put back what has already been discarded.

prompt: On the collection {1, 2, 3}, a relation contains (1,1), (2,2) and (3,3) and nothing else. Is it reflexive?
optionA: No, because no member is related to any other member
optionB: Yes, because every member is related to itself
optionC: Yes, but only for the member 1
optionD: It cannot be decided without seeing more pairs
correctAnswerText: Yes, because every member is related to itself
explanation: Reflexivity asks only that each member relate to itself, and all three do. Whether anything else is present is a separate question about other properties.

prompt: On the collection {1, 2, 3}, a relation contains (1,2), (2,1) and (1,3). Symmetry requires that whenever a pair is present its reverse is present too, and (3,1) is missing while (1,3) is there. Is the relation symmetric?
optionA: Yes, because (1,2) and (2,1) are both present
optionB: Yes, because most of the pairs do have their reverse
optionC: No, because the pair (2,2) is missing
optionD: No, because (1,3) is present without (3,1)
correctAnswerText: No, because (1,3) is present without (3,1)
explanation: One pair without its reverse settles it, whatever the others do. A missing self-pair would bear on reflexivity and says nothing about symmetry.

prompt: On a collection of three members, a relation contains no pairs whatever. Symmetry and transitivity are demands made of pairs that are present, and there are none to violate, while reflexivity demands a pair for each of the three members. Which properties does this relation have?
optionA: Symmetric and transitive, but not reflexive
optionB: None of the three
optionC: All three of them
optionD: Reflexive only
correctAnswerText: Symmetric and transitive, but not reflexive
explanation: Two of the properties are satisfied because nothing can break them, and the third is not because it demands something be present. The empty case separates properties that forbid from properties that require.
